title: Are Africa’s power grids ready for the AI data centre boom?
gist: The World Economic Forum argues Africa's AI-driven data centre demand -- projected by McKinsey to grow from 0.4 GW today to as much as 2.2 GW by 2030 -- will strain power grids unless African governments plan energy and digital infrastructure together now, citing Ireland's reactive grid restrictions and Amsterdam's data centre moratorium as cautionary precedents.

insights.claim: The global AI race is increasingly a contest for access to electricity and grid capacity rather than just algorithms and chips, since AI data centres' dense processors, networks and cooling needs can consume as much electricity as a small city.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Investors assessing AI infrastructure plays should weight grid access and power availability as heavily as chip supply when evaluating data centre buildout risk.
insights.quote: The AI race is becoming a competition for power grids.

insights.claim: A large hyperscale AI/cloud campus can require 100 megawatts or more of power, and such projects often cluster geographically, creating sudden, concentrated demand spikes that outpace typical grid planning cycles.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Grid operators and utility investors should expect lumpy, geographically concentrated demand shocks near AI clusters rather than smooth, predictable load growth.

insights.claim: New transmission lines and substations typically take far longer to permit and construct than the data centre facilities they are meant to serve, creating a structural mismatch between how fast AI infrastructure can be built and how fast power delivery can be scaled.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Permitting and grid-buildout lag, not data centre construction itself, is likely the critical-path bottleneck investors should price into AI infrastructure project timelines.

insights.claim: McKinsey estimates Africa's data centre capacity demand will rise from about 0.4 GW today to between 1.5 and 2.2 GW by 2030, a build-out that would require $10-20 billion in construction investment.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Quantifies a multi-billion-dollar African data centre infrastructure investment opportunity over the next four years.
insights.quote: McKinsey estimates that the continent’s demand for data centre capacity could rise from about 0.4 gigawatts (GW) today to between 1.5 and 2.2 GW by 2030.
insights.locator: Africa's data centre market is accelerating

insights.claim: Combined installed data centre capacity across Africa's five leading markets -- Egypt, Kenya, Morocco, Nigeria and South Africa -- is currently below 500 megawatts, less than France had in 2024, underscoring how early-stage the continent's AI infrastructure buildout still is.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Establishes the low current base from which African data centre capacity growth is being measured, framing the scale of the opportunity and the funding gap.
insights.locator: Africa's data centre market is accelerating

insights.claim: Demand in Africa's five leading data centre markets (Egypt, Kenya, Morocco, Nigeria, South Africa) is expected to grow 3.5 to 5.5 times by the end of the decade, driven by cloud adoption, data sovereignty requirements and AI moving from experimentation into production.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific African markets positioned for the fastest data centre capacity growth this decade, useful for targeting infrastructure investment.
insights.locator: Africa's data centre market is accelerating

insights.claim: About 40% of African corporations are already experimenting with or implementing generative AI across sectors including telecommunications, banking and public services, and as these pilots move into production they will intensify demand for locally hosted computing capacity.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Corporate generative AI adoption is a leading indicator investors can track for near-term African data centre demand growth.
insights.locator: Africa's data centre market is accelerating

insights.claim: In Ireland, data centres already accounted for about 22% of the country's metered electricity consumption by 2024, showing how quickly AI and cloud infrastructure can come to dominate a national grid's load when left unmanaged.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Serves as a benchmark ceiling for how large a share of national electricity data centres can consume in a market without proactive planning -- a useful comparator for forecasting other regions.
insights.quote: In Ireland, data centres already accounted for about 22% of metered electricity consumption by 2024.

insights.claim: Ireland introduced data centre grid connection restrictions in 2021, which were replaced by a new national policy in December 2025 requiring proposed facilities to address their grid impact before being approved.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Signals a regulatory tightening trajectory that other AI-hungry markets may follow, raising future compliance costs and approval delays for data centre developers.

insights.claim: Amsterdam has banned new data centres and expansions until at least 2030, illustrating how delayed grid planning can force regulators into blunt, costly interventions that restrict growth outright.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A cautionary precedent for investors betting on unconstrained data centre expansion in dense markets -- outright regulatory moratoria are a real tail risk when grid planning lags.

insights.claim: The World Bank argues infrastructure investments generate their greatest returns when energy, digital and transport systems are planned together, because electricity makes digital infrastructure productive while digital systems in turn improve how power networks are run.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Investors should favor markets or projects where governments demonstrate cross-sector power-plus-digital planning coordination, as these likely carry lower execution risk.
insights.locator: Planning power and digital infrastructure together

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia is coordinating digital expansion, grid investment and renewables simultaneously; research by the Kingdom's King Abdullah Petroleum Studies and Research Center (KAPSARC) projects its data centre capacity could exceed 1 GW by 2030 and reach about 4.1 GW under a high-growth scenario.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Positions Saudi Arabia as a fast-scaling, state-coordinated AI infrastructure hub -- a comparator and potential competitor case study for other emerging markets, including Africa.

themes.theme: Policy Recommendations and Regional Power Integration

insights.claim: National electricity plans should incorporate credible data centre and AI demand scenarios while accounting for the risk that not every announced project will be built, since overestimating demand risks creating stranded generation and grid assets.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Flags stranded-asset risk as a real downside scenario for African grid buildouts tied to speculative AI demand forecasts.
insights.locator: How countries can satisfy AI demand

insights.claim: About 8% of the West African Power Pool's regional electricity is currently traded across borders; expanding this regional integration would let surplus generation in one country meet AI-driven demand in another, widening the pool of low-cost power available to data centres.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Cross-border power trading capacity in West Africa remains largely underutilized (~8%), representing a potential lever for unlocking cheaper power for data centre investment via deeper regional integration.
insights.locator: How countries can satisfy AI demand

insights.claim: Regulators should set transparent grid connection and cost allocation rules so data centre developers contribute fairly to infrastructure costs rather than shifting the burden onto ordinary household electricity consumers, and governments should back shared digital or industrial zones that pool grid connections to lower costs and strengthen investor confidence.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Cost-allocation and zoning policy design will materially affect data centre project economics in African markets -- investors should watch for developer-pays versus socialized-cost regulatory models and zone-based coordinated infrastructure as a lower-risk entry route.
insights.locator: How countries can satisfy AI demand
